## Objectives

1. Understand the core packages and functions within tidymodels and how they can be used for common forest modeling scenarios. 
2. Be able to design workflows that allow for training and testing models to evaluate and validate their performance.
3. Understand how to work with model output in an efficient manner so that results can be easily interpreted and visualized. 

## tidymodels

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
<br>
![](https://tidymodels.tidymodels.org/logo.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
<br>
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
install.packages("tidymodels")
library(tidymodels)
```
<br>

- A collection of R packages for modeling (e.g., regression, machine learning)
- Uses tidyverse principles (good for data wrangling and visualization)
- Sets up workflows that are reproducible

:::
:::


## tidymodels is a collection of many packages

::: columns

::: {.column}

There are ~8 core packages in `tidymodels`. We'll focus on:

<br> 

* `rsample` - Splits data into training and testing sets 
* `recipes` - Preprocesses data 
* `parsnip` - Specifies models 
* `broom` - Converts model objects into tidy datasets 
* `yardstick` - Assesses model performance 


:::

::: {.column .center}

![](images/tidymodels-pkgs.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="tidymodels packages hex logos" width=100%} 

<small>Image: <a href="https://rpubs.com/chenx/tidymodels_tutorial">rpubs.com/chenx/tidymodels_tutorial</a></small>

:::

:::

## Goal: Predict aboveground tree biomass for various species groups

* There are 114 different species in the dataset
* We will group species into one of 10 Jenkins species groups.

::: columns

::: {.column}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
tree |>  
  group_by(COMMON_NAME) |> 
  summarize(`Num trees` = n(),
            `Mean DBH (cm)` = round(mean(dbh_cm, na.rm=T), 1),
            `Min DBH (cm)` = min(dbh_cm, na.rm=T),
            `Max DBH (cm)` = max(dbh_cm, na.rm=T),
            `Mean weight (kg)`= round(mean(bm_kg, na.rm=T), 1),
            `Min weight (kg)` = min(bm_kg, na.rm=T),
            `Max weight (kg)` = max(bm_kg, na.rm=T)) |> 
  arrange(desc(`Num trees`))
```

:::

::: {.column .center}

![](images/species_list.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="R screenshot showing a summary of 114 species." width=100%} 

:::

:::

## The modeling

| Exercise | Functions |
|:---------|:------|
| Refit a single species group | `workflow()`, `fit()`, `tidy()` |
| Refit to all species groups | `nest()`, `map()` |
| Compare fits to original Jenkins equation | Joining and interpreting coefficients |
| Predict biomass on new sites | Back-transformation |


## The Jenkins equation form

$$
\ln(bm) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln(dbh)
$$

or equivalently, on the original scale:

$$
bm = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln(dbh)} = e^{\beta_0} \cdot dbh^{\beta_1}
$$

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
* $bm$ = total aboveground dry biomass (kg)
* $dbh$ = diameter at breast height (cm)
* $\beta_0, \beta_1$ = coefficients, **one pair per species group**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
* Linear on the log-log scale
* We can use `linear_reg()` 

:::

:::


## `broom`: turns model objects into tidy datasets 

* Model objects from base R (e.g., `lm()`) store results in nested lists. These are awkward to work with.
* `broom` converts model onject output into **tibbles**, so you can use the tidyverse.
* Three key functions:
    * `tidy()` - Extracts model coefficients and related statistics
    * `glance()` - Provides overall model fit statistics
    * `augment()` - Adds predictions and residuals to the original data

## Random forests 

::: columns

::: {.column}
* First, take several small samples of the data
* Any observations that aren’t taken are called “out-of-bag” samples
* Build a set of regression trees on the sampled data and calculate mean square error 
:::

::: {.column .center}

![](images/rf_bootstrap.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="An example of bootstrapped samples from a random forest." width=100%} 

:::

:::

## Variable importance in random forests 

::: columns

::: {.column}
* If the percent increase in MSE after removing the variable is large, it’s an important variable!
* If the percent increase in MSE is small, it’s less important
:::

::: {.column .center}

![](images/rf_importance.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="An example of variable importance in a random forest model." width=100%} 

:::

:::
## Key arguments in `rand_forest()` {.smaller}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}

<br>

| Argument | Meaning | Value |
|:---------|:--------|:----------|
| `trees` | Number of trees in the forest | e.g., 500 |
| `mtry` | Predictors considered at each split | 1 or 2 (DBH or species group) |
| `min_n` | Minimum observations to split a node | e.g., 5 |

:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
<br>
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
rand_forest(
  trees = 500,
  mtry  = 2,
  min_n = 5) |>
  set_engine("ranger",
             importance = "permutation") |>
  set_mode("regression")
```

:::

:::

## How to compare models?


| Metric | Measures | 
|:-------|:---------|
| **RMSE** (kg) | Typical error |
| **MAE** (kg) | Mean absolute error | 
| **Bias** (%) | Systematic over- or under-prediction | 

<br>

* Compute metrics on the original (kg) scale
* Use the held-out (test) data


## The `yardstick` package

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}

* Provides metric functions, e.g., `rmse()`, `mae()`, `rsq()`
* `metric_set()` bundles all metrics using a single function
* Outputs a dataset (i.e., a "tidy tibble")

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Get one metric
rmse(test_pred, 
     truth = bm_kg,
     estimate = rf_kg)

# Get a bundle of metrics
biomass_metrics <- metric_set(rmse, mae, bias)
```
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}

![](images/yardstick.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Hex sticker for yardstick package." width=50%} 

:::

:::
